overview.body:
**Annwn** (*annwn*) — Otherworld, Underworld · the deep, the abyss — is the Welsh Otherworld of the Mabinogi and the oldest Welsh poetry: the realm where [[arawn|Arawn]] rules a court of unsurpassed plenty, where Arthur sailed in Prydwen for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn and lost all but seven of his men, and where Gwyn ap Nudd rides with the hunt that keeps the demons of the deep from destroying this world.[^1]

The name is the place: Middle Welsh *annwfn* resolves as *an-* + *dwfn*, 'the un-deep, the very deep' — the abyss beneath the world, glossed by the University of Wales dictionary simply as 'the otherworld, the abyss'.[^2] It is first met on the page in the opening episode of the First Branch of the Mabinogi, where Pwyll of Dyfed offends Arawn at the hunt in Glyn Cuch and pays the debt with a year spent ruling Annwn in the king's own shape — earning for his reward the title Pwyll Pen Annwn, 'Head of Annwn'.[^1]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Annwn** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Welsh writes no diacritic in this name. The mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography and never about the realm. No domain is claimed: the plain-ASCII **annwn.com** is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.[^3]

sources.citation: Davies, Sioned, trans., The Mabinogion (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007), Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed.
Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru / A Dictionary of the Welsh Language (Cardiff: University of Wales Press, 1950–2002), s.v. annwfn.
Koch, John T., ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia, 5 vols. (Santa Barbara: ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Annwfn.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Middle Welsh as **annwfn** — the spelling of the Book of Taliesin and the Mabinogi manuscripts, where final *-f-* writes the voiced fricative [v] — and in the normalized modern spelling **Annwn** used for the Otherworld ever since.[^1] The University of Wales dictionary glosses the word 'the otherworld, the abyss', and the standard analysis resolves it as the prefix *an-* (negative or intensifying) + *dwfn*, 'deep': the un-deep, the very deep — the meaning this lexicon carries, 'the deep, the abyss'.[^2]

The popular gloss 'not-world' — *an-* + a form of *byd*/*gwyn* heard in the sounds — is a later reinterpretation rather than the philology; the manuscript word is built on *dwfn*, and the abyss, not negation, is the image the texts use: a realm below, entered at a ford or a hunting-clearing, from which voyages return diminished or not at all.[^2]

The ASCII form *annwn* loses nothing, because the normalized Welsh spelling is already plain Latin letters; the restoration is therefore a matter of canonical reference, not rescued diacritics, and the name is classified Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **a** → **A** — Same, capitalized
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **w** → **w** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same

The project holds no domain for this name: **annwn.com** is registered to a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release. The temple lives at its canonical lexicon address.

sources.citation: Evans, J. Gwenogvryn, ed., Facsimile and Text of the Book of Taliesin (Llanbedrog, 1910).
Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru / A Dictionary of the Welsh Language (Cardiff: University of Wales Press, 1950–2002), s.v. annwfn, dwfn.

pronunciation.body:
The modern Welsh pronunciation of the name is **/ˈanʊn/** — Modern Welsh.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **A-** — Short open [a], stressed on the first syllable, as Welsh penultimate stress demands in a two-syllable word
- **-nn-** — Geminate alveolar nasal [nː], written double and held longer than a single English n
- **-w-** — The letter w is here a full vowel: short high back rounded [ʊ], the 'oo' of English 'put' — never a consonant
- **-n** — Final alveolar nasal [n], closing the word cleanly

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'AN-oon' — two syllables, the first stressed, the w sounded as a short 'oo'.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Middle Welsh** — Annwfn, the manuscript spelling, the f writing the voiced [v] of the lenited final consonant
- **Modern Welsh** — Annwn, the normalized living form
- **The compound** — an- + dwfn, 'the un-deep, the very deep'
- **The title it generated** — Pen Annwn, 'Head of Annwn', borne by Pwyll after his year in the realm and by the Otherworld's cauldron-master in the Taliesin poem[^2]

Annwn is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing ASCII loses: the letters of the normalized form are the letters of the keyboard. The capital alone marks the temple form.

sources.citation: Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru / A Dictionary of the Welsh Language (Cardiff: University of Wales Press, 1950–2002), s.v. annwfn, with pronunciation.
Davies, Sioned, trans., The Mabinogion (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007); Haycock, Marged, ed. and trans., Legendary Poems from the Book of Taliesin (Aberystwyth: CMCS, 2007), on Pen Annwfn.

domains.body:
**Annwn** is catalogued under the domain 'Otherworld, Underworld' — the two registers in which the texts actually present it.[^1]

### Otherworld

Annwn is first of all a court: Arawn's realm of unsurpassed plenty, where the feast never fails and the hall is hung with gold and jewels — the place Pwyll ruled for a year in another man's shape and found so well ordered that he never wished to leave it.[^1] The Taliesin poem gives it architecture: Caer Sidi and its sister fortresses, the revolving castles of the deep that Arthur's men assaulted and mostly never left.[^2]

### Underworld

But the name means the deep, and the texts keep the darkness in it. Annwn is the home of the demons over whom God set Gwyn ap Nudd, 'lest this world be destroyed'; its creatures — the white red-eared hounds, the treasures that will not serve a coward — cross into this world only at its edges, and what is taken from it is paid for.[^3]

### The Feast and the Hunt

Two activities define the realm in every source: the feast, boundless but testing — the cauldron of the Head of Annwn will not boil a coward's food — and the hunt, which in Annwn is not sport but custody, the riding-out that keeps the deep's worst inhabitants leashed.[^2][^3]

sources.citation: Davies, Sioned, trans., The Mabinogion (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007), Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed.
Haycock, Marged, ed. and trans., Legendary Poems from the Book of Taliesin (Aberystwyth: CMCS, 2007), Preiddeu Annwfn.
Bromwich, Rachel, and D. Simon Evans, eds., Culhwch and Olwen: An Edition and Study (Cardiff: University of Wales Press, 1992).

symbols.body:
Annwn's attributes are the few fixed images the Welsh tradition never varies — each a boundary made visible:[^1]

- **The cauldron of Pen Annwn** — Kindled by the breath of nine maidens, its rim set with pearls, and ruled by the law of Otherworld vessels: it will not boil the food of a coward[^2]
- **The white hounds with red ears** — Arawn's pack at Glyn Cuch, gleaming white with red ears: the colours Welsh tradition gives every creature out of the Otherworld[^1]
- **Caer Sidi and the fortresses** — The revolving castle and its sisters, the Otherworld as fortifications that must be won rather than visited[^2]
- **Prydwen** — Arthur's ship on the raid of Preiddeu Annwfn: three full loads went into the deep, and except seven none returned[^2]
- **The year's exchange** — Arawn and Pwyll trading shapes, kingdoms, and beds for a year and a day: the Otherworld close enough to wear a man's face[^1]

sources.citation: Davies, Sioned, trans., The Mabinogion (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007), Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed.
Haycock, Marged, ed. and trans., Legendary Poems from the Book of Taliesin (Aberystwyth: CMCS, 2007), Preiddeu Annwfn.

mythology.body:
Annwn's dossier is concentrated in four witnesses — the First Branch of the Mabinogi, the Taliesin poem Preiddeu Annwfn, the hunting catalogue of Culhwch ac Olwen, and the Welsh Life of St Collen.[^1]

### The Year in Annwn (Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed)

Hunting in Glyn Cuch, Pwyll of Dyfed drives a strange pack off a stag — hounds gleaming white, with red ears — and feeds his own dogs on the kill. The pack's master is [[arawn|Arawn]], a king of Annwn, and the debt is settled by a bargain: the two exchange shapes and kingdoms for a year and a day, and at the year's end Pwyll must strike down Arawn's rival Hafgan, who can be killed by one blow only. Pwyll rules Annwn in Arawn's likeness, lies chaste beside Arawn's queen every night of the year, strikes Hafgan once at the ford and refuses the second blow, and returns to Glyn Cuch to trade shapes back. The friendship is sealed with gifts, and Pwyll is ever after called Pwyll Pen Annwn — Head of Annwn.[^1]

### The Spoils of Annwfn (Book of Taliesin)

Preiddeu Annwfn, spoken by the poet [[taliesin|Taliesin]] himself, is the oldest Arthurian Otherworld raid. Arthur sails in Prydwen against the fortresses of the deep — Caer Sidi, Caer Pedryfan, Caer Wydyr — for the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn, kindled by the breath of nine maidens and rimmed with pearls, which will not boil a coward's food. The refrain tolls after each fortress: except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.[^2]

### Gwyn ap Nudd and the Demons (Culhwch ac Olwen)

The hunting catalogue of Culhwch ac Olwen names the realm's huntsman: Gwyn ap Nudd, 'in whom God set the essence of the demons of Annwn, lest this world be destroyed' — conscripted to the hunt of Twrch Trwyth because without him it cannot be done. The same tale fixes his standing quarrel with Gwythyr ap Greidawl over Creiddylad daughter of Lludd: Arthur judged that the two fight for her every May Day until the Day of Judgment.[^3]

### The Court on the Tor (Buchedd Collen)

The Life of St Collen gives Annwn its local address: Gwyn ap Nudd, king of Annwn and of the Fair Folk, keeps a castle of utmost splendour on Glastonbury Tor and feasts the saint on dishes beyond earthly measure — until Collen's holy water disperses castle, court, and king, leaving him standing on the green hill.[^4]

syncretism.body:
Annwn's clearest kin are Irish, and the comparison is structural rather than genealogical: no Irish text knows the name, but the síd of the Túatha Dé Danann matches its profile point for point. The standing parallel is the cauldron: [[dagda|the Dagda]]'s cauldron of Murias, from which no company ever went away unsatisfied, is the Irish face of the vessel of plenty that in Wales becomes the cauldron of the Head of Annwn — and Mac Cana sets the two side by side as one Celtic figure-type.[^1] The Irish Otherworld of the immrama and echtrai — Mag Mell, Emain Ablach under [[manannan|Manannán]], lands without grief, sorrow, or death — supplies the same profile of plenty and suspended age that the Welsh sources give Annwn.

Within the Welsh corpus itself, Annwn's borders touch the other Otherworldly episodes of the Mabinogi: the Dyfed of [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] and the enchanted Desolation of [[manawydan|Manawydan]] are told in the same idiom of a world one courtesy away from ours. The Christian redactors re-labelled without restructuring: by Buchedd Collen, Gwyn ap Nudd's court could be dismissed as a demonic glamour while every detail of the feast was preserved intact — and Culhwch had already made the demons of Annwn a standing threat that only Gwyn's custody restrains.[^2]

sources.citation: Mac Cana, Proinsias, Celtic Mythology (London: Hamlyn, 1970), on the cauldron of plenty and the Insular Otherworld.
Bromwich, Rachel, and D. Simon Evans, eds., Culhwch and Olwen (Cardiff: University of Wales Press, 1992); Buchedd Collen, in Baring-Gould and Fisher, Lives of the British Saints, vol. 2 (1908).

cultural-legacy.body:
Preiddeu Annwfn stands at the head of the Arthurian tradition: the raid on the fortresses of the deep is older than every romance of the Grail, and scholars from Loomis onward have read the quest for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn — a vessel of plenty that tests the worthy — as the Grail story's deepest Welsh root.[^1] The comparison with [[dagda|the Dagda]]'s cauldron and the Welsh pairperi keeps Annwn at the centre of every account of the Celtic vessel of plenty.

In Welsh itself the name never went anywhere: *Annwn* remains the living word for the Otherworld, and the white red-eared hounds became the Cŵn Annwn of later folklore, the pack whose crying in the night sky foretells a death.[^2] Gwyn ap Nudd rode out of the texts into modern Druidry and pagan practice as the great huntsman of the Welsh tradition, and Glastonbury Tor — crowned now by the stump of St Michael's tower — still carries his court in the popular imagination. Modern editions and translations — Williams's Pedeir Keinc, Davies's Oxford Mabinogion, Haycock's Taliesin poems — have made the realm a fixed point of Celtic studies.[^3]

sources.citation: Mac Cana, Proinsias, Celtic Mythology (London: Hamlyn, 1970); Koch, John T., ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Annwfn, Preiddeu Annwfn.
MacKillop, James, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998), s.v. Annwn, Cŵn Annwn.

archaeology.body:
Annwn is a wholly textual realm: no inscription invokes it, and the Romano-British epigraphy of Wales is silent on the Otherworld by name.[^1] Its manuscript witnesses, however, are exact. The Mabinogi survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1400), the two great codices of medieval Welsh prose; Preiddeu Annwfn is preserved uniquely in the Book of Taliesin (National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century); and Culhwch ac Olwen comes down in a White Book fragment and the full Red Book text.[^2]

The one site the tradition ties to Annwn is Glastonbury Tor, Gwyn ap Nudd's seat in Buchedd Collen. Excavations on the Tor in the 1960s found sub-Roman and early medieval occupation beneath the ruins of the medieval church of St Michael — real archaeology on the hill, though none of it speaks to the Otherworld, whose only true location is the text.[^3]

sources.citation: Koch, John T., ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Annwfn.
Williams, Ifor, ed., Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930), introduction; Evans, J. Gwenogvryn, ed., Facsimile and Text of the Book of Taliesin (1910).
Rahtz, Philip, and Lorna Watts, Glastonbury: Myth and Archaeology (Stroud: Tempus, 2003), on the Tor excavations.

meditation.body:
Annwn is the rare Otherworld whose name tells you where it is: an- + dwfn, the un-deep, the very deep — not a land over the sea or under a hill but the depth beneath the world, the place the surface world is the skin of. The tradition never pretends it is far away. Pwyll stumbles into it on an ordinary hunt by breaking an ordinary courtesy; it lies a year's shape-shift away, close enough for two kings to trade faces and governments across it.[^1]

And its gifts all carry a price exacted in courage. The feast is boundless, but the cauldron will not boil a coward's food; the voyage is possible, but except seven none returned; the hunt rides out, but it rides to keep the demons of the deep leashed for the world's sake.[^2] Annwn is the Celtic imagination's answer to the question of what lies underneath: plenty without limit, behind a door that opens only once — and a word for it, five plain letters, that still means the deep.

sources.citation: Davies, Sioned, trans., The Mabinogion (Oxford University Press, 2007), Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed.
Haycock, Marged, ed. and trans., Legendary Poems from the Book of Taliesin (CMCS, 2007), Preiddeu Annwfn.

irish-cycles.body:
The Welsh Otherworld has no Irish name, but it has an Irish twin. The **síd** — the hollow hills of the Túatha Dé Danann — matches Annwn's profile point for point: a realm of boundless feast and suspended age, entered at a ford, a hunting-mound, or over the sea, from which visitors return diminished, centuries older, or not at all.[^1] Irish geography scatters the Otherworld across named lands: **Emain Ablach**, the island of apple-trees ruled by [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]]; **Mag Mell**, the plain of delight where there is neither grief nor sorrow nor death; and **Tech Duinn**, the house of Donn off the south-western shore, where the dead of Ireland gather for the final journey.[^2]

The Irish literature of reaching such places is the **immram**, the voyage-tale, and its two great exemplars are preserved in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow. In *Immram Brain*, Bran mac Febail is summoned by an Otherworld woman bearing a silver apple-branch to the Land of Women, and returns to find his name already a distant memory; in *Immram Curaig Maíle Dúin*, the hero's coracle crosses a catalogue of wonder-islands, each of them a lesson in the Otherworld's laws.[^3]

**Preiddeu Annwfn** belongs to this same tradition: Mac Cana reads the Taliesin poem — Arthur's raid by ship on the fortresses of the deep, the refrain 'except seven none returned' — as the Welsh witness of the immram pattern, an Otherworld voyage told from the raider's side.[^4] And the prize Arthur sought has its exact Irish counterpart: the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, which will not boil a coward's food, is the functional twin of the [[dagda|Dagda]]'s cauldron of Murias, from which no company ever went away unsatisfied — the two Insular faces of one Celtic vessel of plenty.[^1][^4]

Sims-Williams has shown that such parallels are not borrowings to be inventoried but the common Insular inheritance of two literatures in constant contact; the honest comparison is structural, and it leaves Annwn neither derived from the síd nor independent of the world that imagined it.[^5]

welsh-sources.body:
Annwn is a Welsh word and a Welsh realm, and its dossier is drawn from the four strata of the Welsh corpus. The prose Mabinogi — the Four Branches, preserved in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest — gives the realm its narrative form: [[arawn|Arawn]]'s court, the year's exchange, the title Pen Annwn that Pwyll carries back to Dyfed.[^1] The verse stratum is older and harder: Preiddeu Annwfn, the Taliesin poem of the Book of Taliesin, speaks the raid in the poet's own voice and names the fortresses, the cauldron, and the seven who returned.[^2]

The Arthurian catalogue stratum adds the hunt: Culhwch ac Olwen, preserved with the Mabinogi in the Red Book, places Gwyn ap Nudd over the demons of Annwn and fixes his May Day war with Gwythyr for Creiddylad daughter of Lludd.[^3] The hagiographic stratum comes last and changes nothing essential: Buchedd Collen moves the court to Glastonbury Tor, calls Gwyn king of Annwn and of the Fair Folk, and lets a saint's holy water dispel the feast — the Christian frame laid over the pagan facts without altering one of them.[^4]

Haycock, Marged, ed. and trans., Legendary Poems from the Book of Taliesin (CMCS, 2007).
Bromwich, Rachel, and D. Simon Evans, eds., Culhwch and Olwen (University of Wales Press, 1992).
Buchedd Collen, in Baring-Gould and Fisher, Lives of the British Saints, vol. 2 (1908).

inscriptions.body:
No inscription names Annwn. Wales in the Roman and early medieval periods left a substantial epigraphic record — Latin memorial stones of the fifth to seventh centuries, and a smaller body of ogham-and-Latin bilinguals in the Irish-settled south-west — but the surviving stones carry personal names in formulaic commemorations, not cosmology, and no reading of Annwn has ever been proposed for any of them.[^1]

The word's first secure attestation is therefore literary: the Book of Taliesin, where Preiddeu Annwfn already treats the realm, its fortresses, and its cauldron as matters a courtly audience knows. The silence of the stones is characteristic of the Insular Celtic record, whose paganism left place-names and literature rather than dedications — the deep was sung, not carved.[^2]

sources.citation: Nash-Williams, V. E., The Early Christian Monuments of Wales (Cardiff: University of Wales Press, 1950).
Haycock, Marged, ed. and trans., Legendary Poems from the Book of Taliesin (CMCS, 2007), introduction.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Welsh manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **annwfn** — Middle Welsh in Insular script, attested from the Book of Taliesin (early fourteenth century) onward, with the Mabinogi and Culhwch witnesses in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest.[^1] Welsh has used the Latin alphabet throughout its written history; the earlier epigraphic record is Latin and ogham memorial stones, neither of which preserves this word.[^2]

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- Middle Welsh writes the name *annwfn*, the f writing the voiced fricative [v]; the normalized modern spelling is **Annwn**.
- The dictionary analysis resolves the compound as *an-* + *dwfn*, 'deep' — 'the un-deep, the very deep'; the gloss 'not-world' is a later popular reinterpretation of the same sounds.[^3]
- The letter w is a full vowel in Welsh ([ʊ]); nothing in the spelling requires a diacritic, so nothing distinctive is lost in ASCII.
- The Unicode restoration Annwn is therefore identical to the ASCII form apart from the capital; the temple form is a canonical reference, not a rescued spelling.

One caution attaches to the record: the 'f' of the manuscript form is consonantal [v], but the modern normalized spelling drops it — a regular outcome of Welsh final-consonant loss, not an editorial liberty.[^3]

sources.citation: Evans, J. Gwenogvryn, ed., Facsimile and Text of the Book of Taliesin (1910); Williams, Ifor, ed., Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930).
Nash-Williams, V. E., The Early Christian Monuments of Wales (University of Wales Press, 1950).
Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru / A Dictionary of the Welsh Language (University of Wales Press, 1950–2002), s.v. annwfn, dwfn.
